explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: The bind address alone doesn't tell you the actual reachability -- a firewall rule can already restrict a 0.0.0.0-bound service to the LAN only, which this check has no visibility into; it only reports the bind address, not the effective exposure after firewalling.

worked_example.scenario: A listening socket: process 'node.exe', bound to 0.0.0.0:8080.
walkthrough: 0.0.0.0 is in the 'any address' set -- the check warns, listing this listener among the broad-bound set.

explanations.title: What 'no high-risk legacy service ports are reachable' checks
explanations.plain: Ports like FTP (21), Telnet (23), SMB (445), and RDP (3389) are the most commonly scanned-for and exploited services on the internet and on LANs alike. One reachable on a non-loopback address is a standing target for automated exploitation tooling, not a theoretical risk.
explanations.how_it_decides: Enumerates listening sockets and flags any bound to something other than 127.0.0.1/::1 on one of a fixed high-risk port list (21, 23, 135, 139, 445, 1433, 1434, 3306, 3389, 5432, 5900, 6379, 27017). Any match is a fail, naming the service and port.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: Some of these ports (5432 PostgreSQL, 3306 MySQL, 6379 Redis, 27017 MongoDB) are entirely legitimate for a development machine that's deliberately running a local database server -- the risk is real specifically when it's reachable beyond loopback, which is exactly what this check measures, not the mere presence of the service.

worked_example.scenario: A listening socket: SMB on 0.0.0.0:445.
walkthrough: 0.0.0.0 is not loopback, and 445 is in the high-risk port set (labeled 'SMB') -- the check fails, naming 'SMB (445)' as reachable on a non-loopback address.

explanations.title: What 'no unexpected processes are listening for inbound connections' checks
explanations.plain: Most user-installed software has no business accepting inbound network connections at all. A process you don't recognise with an open listening socket is one of the more reliable signals of malware, a forgotten dev server, or bundled remote-access software you didn't intend to run.
explanations.how_it_decides: Compares each listening socket's owning process name against a small baseline of processes expected to listen on a fresh Windows install (System, svchost.exe, lsass.exe, services.exe, and similar). Anything outside that baseline is a warn, not a fail -- this is explicitly informational, meant for your own review, not a verdict.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: Ordinary, entirely legitimate software -- a game server, a local dev server, sync software, this very tool -- listens for inbound connections as part of normal operation and isn't in the tiny system baseline; a warn here is the expected, common case on almost any real machine, not evidence of a problem.

worked_example.scenario: A listening socket owned by 'python.exe', a local dev server on 127.0.0.1:8000.
walkthrough: 'python.exe' isn't in the expected-listener baseline -- the check warns, listing it among unexpected listeners, purely for your own review.

explanations.title: What 'UPnP discovery/port-mapping services are disabled' checks
explanations.plain: UPnP lets any device or piece of software on the LAN ask this machine, or the router, to automatically open inbound ports, with no authentication at all. It's a convenience feature that doubles as a standing invitation for malware or a compromised IoT device on the same network to punch a hole outward.
explanations.how_it_decides: Reads the status of the SSDPSRV and upnphost services. Either one Running is a warn, listing which -- not a fail, since UPnP does have genuine convenience uses (game console connectivity, some media devices).
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: Plenty of home setups genuinely rely on UPnP for game consoles, casting devices, and some media/smart-home apps to work without manual port-forwarding -- disabling it can break that connectivity, which is exactly why this is a warn rather than an unconditional fail.

worked_example.scenario: SSDPSRV: Status=Running; upnphost: Status=Running.
walkthrough: Both services running -- the check warns, naming both.

explanations.title: What 'Microsoft Defender real-time protection is enabled' checks
explanations.plain: Real-time protection is what catches malware at write/execute time, before it has a chance to act. With it off, this machine is only ever scanned on whatever schedule you remember to run manually -- most infections would be caught in the exact seconds it's off, not found afterwards.
explanations.how_it_decides: Reads RealTimeProtectionEnabled from Get-MpComputerStatus. Exactly True is a pass; anything else is a fail.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: If another antivirus product is installed and active, Windows may deliberately keep Defender's real-time engine off to avoid the two products conflicting -- worth checking for a genuinely active third-party AV before treating this fail as unprotected rather than differently protected.

worked_example.scenario: Get-MpComputerStatus reports RealTimeProtectionEnabled=False, AntivirusEnabled=True.
walkthrough: RealTimeProtectionEnabled isn't True -- the check fails, even though overall antivirus is enabled, because real-time protection specifically is off.

explanations.title: What 'Defender signatures are current' checks
explanations.plain: Signature-based detection is only as good as its last update. Signatures more than a week old miss every threat catalogued since then -- an antivirus running on stale signatures gives a false sense of protection.
explanations.how_it_decides: Reads AntivirusSignatureAge and AntispywareSignatureAge (in days) from Get-MpComputerStatus, and fails if the older of the two exceeds 7 days. Neither age being reported at all is an error, not an assumed pass.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: A machine that's been offline (travel, storage) for over a week will fail this the moment it reconnects, purely from elapsed time, before Windows Update has had a chance to catch up -- the fix in that case is just letting it update, not evidence of a deeper misconfiguration.

worked_example.scenario: AntivirusSignatureAge=9, AntispywareSignatureAge=6.
walkthrough: max(9, 6) = 9, which is > 7 -- the check fails: 'Signatures are 9 day(s) old'.

explanations.title: What 'Windows Update has installed updates recently' checks
explanations.plain: Patch age is a direct measure of exposure to every publicly disclosed vulnerability fixed since the last successful update -- attackers routinely weaponise a patched CVE within days of its Patch Tuesday disclosure, specifically targeting machines that haven't updated yet.
explanations.how_it_decides: Reads the registry's LastSuccessTime for Windows Update installs, parses it, and fails if more than 45 days have elapsed since. An unparseable or missing timestamp is an error, not an assumed pass or fail.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: A machine that's been powered off or offline for an extended stretch (long trip, seasonal storage) will naturally fail this on reconnection purely due to elapsed time -- the remediation (install pending updates) resolves it either way, but the cause isn't necessarily neglect.

worked_example.scenario: LastSuccessTime parses to 60 days ago.
walkthrough: 60 > 45 (UPDATE_MAX_AGE_DAYS) -- the check fails: 'Last successful update was 60 day(s) ago'.

explanations.title: What 'User Account Control is enabled' checks
explanations.plain: UAC is the boundary between a standard user token and an elevated administrator token. With it off, every process a logged-in administrator runs -- including malware tricked into being launched -- runs fully elevated with no prompt at all.
explanations.how_it_decides: Reads EnableLUA from the registry. Exactly 1 is a pass; anything else is a fail.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: There's essentially no legitimate reason to run with UAC off on a modern machine -- some genuinely ancient software written before UAC existed may start prompting or misbehaving once it's back on, which is a compatibility cost worth knowing about, not a reason the fail itself is wrong.

worked_example.scenario: EnableLUA reads 0.
walkthrough: Not equal to 1 -- the check fails: 'EnableLUA = 0 (UAC is disabled)'.

explanations.title: What 'the system drive is BitLocker-protected' checks
explanations.plain: Without disk encryption, anyone with physical access to this machine can remove the drive, mount it on another computer, and read every file on it -- including cached credentials and browser data -- with no need to log in at all.
explanations.how_it_decides: Reads Get-BitLockerVolume (given extra time budget -- this WMI provider is measurably slower than a plain Get-* cmdlet) and checks the system volume's ProtectionStatus. 'On' is a pass; anything else is a fail. If no volumes are returned at all while not running elevated, that's an error with a specific admin hint, since this cmdlet is known to be unreliable without elevation on some Windows editions -- the check would rather say 'can't tell, try elevated' than guess.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: Windows 11 Home doesn't include BitLocker at all (only the narrower-requirements Device Encryption), and BitLocker itself needs a TPM or a USB key on some editions -- an error or fail here can reflect what the specific edition/hardware supports, not necessarily a choice not to encrypt.

worked_example.scenario: Running unelevated; Get-BitLockerVolume returns no volumes.
walkthrough: No system volumes found, and the scan wasn't elevated -- the check errors with an explicit hint to re-run as Administrator, rather than reporting an unverified pass or fail.

explanations.title: What 'the built-in Guest account is disabled' checks
explanations.plain: Guest is a well-known, unauthenticated or trivially-authenticated local account name that attackers try first. Left enabled, it's a free foothold for anything on the network that can reach an SMB or logon surface on this machine.
explanations.how_it_decides: Looks up the local user named 'Guest'. If it doesn't exist at all, the check is 'skipped'. If it exists and Enabled is true, that's a fail; disabled is a pass.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: There is essentially no legitimate reason to keep Guest enabled on a personally administered machine -- this is one of the more clear-cut fails in the catalogue.

worked_example.scenario: Local user 'Guest' exists with Enabled=True.
walkthrough: Guest account is enabled -- the check fails.

explanations.title: What 'the local Administrators group has a small, expected membership' checks
explanations.plain: Every account in the Administrators group is a full compromise of this machine if that one account's credentials leak. Each additional admin -- a forgotten service account, an old installer-created account -- is another way in that gets easier to lose track of over time.
explanations.how_it_decides: Enumerates Administrators group membership and warns if the count exceeds 2 (_MAX_EXPECTED_ADMINS) -- never a fail, since this is a soft threshold rather than a binary misconfiguration, and some machines genuinely need more than two.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: A shared family machine, or one with a separate account for day-to-day use plus a true admin account, commonly has more than two legitimate admin members without anything being wrong -- this check flags count, not identity, and is meant as a prompt to review who's actually in the group.

worked_example.scenario: Administrators group has 4 members.
walkthrough: 4 > 2 (_MAX_EXPECTED_ADMINS) -- the check warns, listing all 4 names.

explanations.title: What 'no local account allows a blank password' checks
explanations.plain: An account with PasswordRequired = False can be logged into -- locally, over RDP if enabled, or via SMB -- with no password at all. It's the same exposure as a leaked credential, except nothing needed to leak in the first place.
explanations.how_it_decides: Checks every enabled local user's PasswordRequired flag. Any enabled account with PasswordRequired = False is a fail, naming every such account.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: This only sees the PasswordRequired flag itself, not whether the account is otherwise unusable (disabled shell, no network logon rights) -- a genuinely locked-down blank-password account would still show as a fail here even if some other control happens to limit its practical reach.

worked_example.scenario: Enabled user 'ServiceAcct' has PasswordRequired=False.
walkthrough: PasswordRequired is False on an enabled account -- the check fails, naming 'ServiceAcct'.

explanations.title: What 'automatic logon is disabled' checks
explanations.plain: Automatic logon skips the login prompt entirely -- anyone who can power on or restart this machine gets a fully logged-in session with no credentials at all. If it's configured with a stored password, that password sits in the registry in plaintext, readable by any process or account that can read HKLM.
explanations.how_it_decides: Reads AutoAdminLogon and whether a DefaultPassword value is stored. AutoAdminLogon='1' with a stored DefaultPassword is a fail, explicitly calling out the plaintext-password case as worse. AutoAdminLogon='1' alone (no stored password) is still a fail, just without that specific extra detail. Neither condition is a pass.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: There's no legitimate justification for a stored plaintext password specifically -- but automatic logon itself, without a stored password, is sometimes a deliberate choice on a kiosk-type machine with no sensitive data and no other users who could reach it physically; the check still fails that case, since the physical-access risk is real regardless of the reason.

worked_example.scenario: AutoAdminLogon='1', DefaultPassword is present in the registry.
walkthrough: AutoAdminLogon is '1' and a password is stored -- the check fails, specifically noting the plaintext password: 'Automatic logon is enabled with a plaintext password stored in the registry'.

explanations.title: What 'throughput (bps)' means
explanations.plain: How much data is actually moving right now, measured in bits per second -- what NetAudit observed, not the theoretical capacity of your connection, which it has no way to measure directly.
explanations.how_it_decides: Computed as bytes observed in a short window, converted to bits (x8) and divided by the window's length in seconds. NetAudit reports both directions (in/out) and totals across the windows it tracks (5 minutes up to 24 hours).
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: A short averaging window makes throughput look spikier than it 'really' is; a longer one smooths out real bursts. Neither is wrong -- they're answering slightly different questions ('what's happening right now' vs 'what's typical').

worked_example.scenario: 1,250,000 bytes are observed moving outbound over a 10-second window.

explanations.title: What 'coefficient of variation' (CV) means
explanations.plain: A single number that says how spread out a set of values is, relative to their own average -- the statistic several detectors use to ask 'how regular is this timing (or size)?'.
explanations.how_it_decides: CV = standard deviation / mean. A CV near 0 means the values are almost identical to each other (very regular); a CV of 1.0 means the spread is as large as the average itself (very irregular). It's unitless, which is what makes it comparable across completely different scales -- a CV of 0.02 on 60-second gaps means the same 'how regular' thing as a CV of 0.02 on 5-minute gaps.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: CV becomes unstable and hard to interpret with very few samples, or when the mean is close to zero -- which is exactly why beaconing-style detectors require a minimum contact count before computing it at all, rather than trusting a CV computed from two or three data points.

worked_example.scenario: Inter-arrival gaps of 60, 61, 59, 60, 61, 59, 60 seconds (7 gaps).
walkthrough: CV = 0.756 / 60.0 ~= 0.0126 -- very regular, well under a typical 0.15 beaconing threshold.

explanations.title: What '(Shannon) entropy' means, in this tool
explanations.plain: A measure, in bits, of how unpredictable a string looks character by character -- used to tell 'real word/name' apart from 'looks randomly generated', which is exactly the distinction dns_tunneling and dga_domains are built around.
explanations.how_it_decides: For a string, entropy = -sum(p(c) * log2(p(c))) over each distinct character c, where p(c) is that character's frequency in the string. A string using few, repeated characters has low entropy (predictable); one using many different characters roughly evenly has high entropy (closer to random). English words typically sit somewhere in the middle; a long block of random hex or base32 sits noticeably higher.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: Entropy alone doesn't know the difference between 'malicious DGA output' and 'legitimate hashed asset filename' or 'CDN edge hostname' -- both are high-entropy by the same measure, which is exactly the documented false-positive case for both dns_tunneling and dga_domains.

worked_example.scenario: The label 'xqzfpltbvk' (10 characters, all distinct).
walkthrough: Each of the 10 characters appears exactly once, so each has probability 1/10.
Entropy = -10 * (1/10 * log2(1/10)) = -log2(0.1) ~= 3.32 bits per character.
Compare to a repetitive string like 'aaaaaaaaaa': entropy = 0 (fully predictable).

explanations.title: What 'confidence' means on a finding
explanations.plain: How sure the detector or rule is that what it found is actually significant, expressed as 0 to 1 (or shown as a percentage) -- separate from severity, which is about how bad the finding would be *if* it's real.
explanations.how_it_decides: Each detector/rule computes confidence its own way -- some combine multiple independent signals (more agreeing signals, higher confidence), some scale directly with a statistic like CV (c2_beaconing: a lower, more regular CV pushes confidence up), and some are close to fixed (a firm port-based match like credentials_plaintext on FTP). There's no single formula across the whole catalogue -- each explanation here documents its own.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: Confidence reflects how well the *pattern* matches, not whether the underlying activity is actually malicious -- a software update checker can produce a beaconing pattern the detector is highly confident about, and be completely benign. High confidence is 'this is definitely the pattern', not 'this is definitely bad'.

explanations.title: What 'severity' means on a finding
explanations.plain: How bad the underlying issue would be if it's a real, confirmed problem -- independent of how likely it is to actually be one. The vocabulary across this whole tool is critical, high, medium, low, info.
explanations.how_it_decides: For posture checks, severity is fixed per check (it describes the risk of that category of misconfiguration existing at all, e.g. blank_passwords is critical, wifi_open_networks_saved is medium) and doesn't change based on the specific evidence found. For threats and recommendations, severity is set per finding based on what was actually observed (e.g. listening_exposed rates SMB/RDP higher than an unrecognised port).
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: Severity says nothing about certainty -- a critical-severity finding with low confidence (a plausible but unconfirmed pattern) can be less urgent in practice than a medium-severity finding the tool is completely sure about. D6's prioritisation combines both, rather than sorting on severity alone.

explanations.title: What 'risk' means, distinct from severity and confidence
explanations.plain: The practical, combined sense of 'how much does this actually matter, right now, on this machine' -- informally, something like severity multiplied by how sure the tool is (confidence) and how easy it would be for someone to actually exploit it.
explanations.how_it_decides: This tool doesn't compute a single universal 'risk' number the way it computes severity or confidence individually -- where you see a risk-flavoured ranking (most concretely, D6's impact_score in /api/findings/prioritised), it's derived from severity, status/confidence, how cheap the fix is, and -- for a documented, specific set of findings -- whether the issue is itself a well-known, credential-free attack path.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: Any single risk number necessarily compresses several different judgements into one -- it's a starting point for what to look at first, not a replacement for reading the actual finding and deciding whether it matters in your specific situation.

explanations.title: What a finding's 'deep link' means
explanations.plain: A pointer telling the dashboard exactly where to take you to see this finding in context -- which view to open, and which specific item to highlight or scroll to within it.
explanations.how_it_decides: Two parts: `view` (one of overview, traffic-log, connections, recommendations, posture, threats) and `id` (the specific item's own id within that view). The frontend uses this to jump straight there instead of leaving you to find it manually.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: A deep link can go stale if the item it points to has since been resolved, acknowledged, or aged out (a threat, for instance, can move to 'resolved' after its cooldown) -- following one to nothing found usually means the underlying issue is no longer current, not that the link itself is broken.

explanations.title: What a finding's 'evidence' list means
explanations.plain: The specific, concrete facts a check or finding is based on -- the actual observed values, not just the conclusion drawn from them.
explanations.how_it_decides: A list of label/value pairs (e.g. {'label': 'RequireSecuritySignature', 'value': 'False'}) attached directly to the raw data a check read or a detector measured, so you can verify the reasoning yourself rather than take the pass/fail/severity at face value.
explanations.what_would_make_it_wrong: Evidence is a snapshot at the moment the check or detector ran -- if you fix the underlying issue, the evidence shown for a past finding doesn't retroactively update; re-running the check is what confirms the fix took effect.
